content: Physical inactivity is a significant contributor to obesity and associated health conditions, including diabetes, poor mental health, and cardiovascular issues. Unsafe building materials, substandard construction practices, or homes built in hazardous locations can expose individuals to risks such as injuries from structural collapses. Housing in slums or informal settlements, as defined by UN-Habitat, poses unique health risks. Currently, approximately one billion people live in slum conditions, often due to exclusion from urban planning processes. According to UN-Habitat, a slum household is defined as a group of individuals living under one roof in an urban area that lacks one or more of the following: durable housing that protects from the elements, sufficient living space, secure tenure, adequate sanitation and infrastructure, and access to uncontaminated water sources. Residents of slums face numerous housing-related risks, including structurally unsafe dwellings, inadequate facilities, overcrowding, poor sanitation, unsafe electrical connections, toxic building materials, unventilated cooking facilities, and unsafe infrastructure such as roads. Additionally, these settlements are often located in areas prone to hazards like landslides, floods, and industrial pollution. The lack of legal ownership of homes in these areas creates stress and increases the risk of forced evictions. Slums and informal settlements frequently house migrants, refugees, and internally displaced persons, with global migration at an all-time high. There are currently an estimated one billion migrants worldwide, including 250 million international migrants and 763 million internal migrants. Among these, 65 million people have been forcibly displaced and urgently require housing solutions. Globally, many people live in poor housing conditions. For example, 4% of the European Union population lives in overcrowded housing with more than three people per room. Approximately 9% of the global population lacks access to improved drinking water sources, with nearly half of those affected residing in sub-Saharan Africa and one-fifth in South Asia. Furthermore, 41% of the global population relies on open fires or simple stoves burning solid fuels for cooking and heating, leading to indoor air pollution and inadequate ventilation. Structural defects in housing are also widespread; for instance, 15% of Europeans live in homes with leaking roofs, damp walls, or rotting structural elements. In the UK, 72% of adults with mobility issues report that their housing is not properly accessible. Poor housing conditions contribute significantly to the global burden of disease. In 2016, inadequate water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) were responsible for 829,000 deaths from diarrheal diseases. Household air pollution from solid fuel use for cooking caused 1.8 million deaths globally, predominantly in lowand middle-income countries. In Europe, 15% of new childhood asthma cases are attributed to indoor dampness, resulting in over 69,000 avoidable disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) and 103 preventable deaths annually. In India, over 2,600 deaths and numerous injuries were recorded in 2012 due to the collapse of more than 2,700 buildings. Vulnerable populations, including those with low incomes, are disproportionately affected by unhealthy housing conditions. For example, in Cambodia, only 29% of households in the lowest income quintile have access to toilet facilities, compared to 79% in the highest income quintile. In Guatemala, 89% of low-income households have dirt floors, compared to just 4% of high-income households. In the United States, repeated hospitalizations for childhood asthma are strongly associated with living in overcrowded housing in areas with high poverty and racial minority populations. Addressing housing-related health risks is essential for breaking the cycle of poor health and economic outcomes. High housing costs can force individuals to cut back on other essentials, such as food, energy, and healthcare, further compromising their health. Interventions to create healthy homes can yield long-term benefits, including improved health, educational outcomes, and economic stability. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed Housing and Health Guidelines (HHGL) to provide evidence-based recommendations for improving housing conditions and reducing health risks. These guidelines emphasize the importance of addressing multiple housing-related risks simultaneously to maximize co-benefits and cost-effectiveness. For example, improving thermal insulation and ventilation can enhance indoor air quality, reduce energy costs, and lower carbon emissions. The HHGL also align with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including SDG 3 (ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being) and SDG 11 (making cities inclusive, safe, resilient, and sustainable). While the guidelines provide global recommendations, their implementation will require adaptation to local contexts. By addressing housing-related health risks, the HHGL aim to improve population health, reduce inequalities, and support sustainable development.
